body: Singapore is a highly developed, clean, and orderly city-state. Its main roads are often divided with black-and-white curbs and double yellow outside lines, and you will frequently see tall apartment blocks. This general appearance is often enough to identify Singapore.
Singaporean street name signs have a unique format: they are green with rounded edges and a distinct white font.

Most Singaporean licence plates are black with white text and are not divided into sections, unlike in Malaysia and Indonesia. You might also see British-style white-and-yellow plates or, very rarely, red plates.
Directional signs are green with white letters in English. A key feature is that expressways are identified by a three-letter code (e.g., TPE).
A unique feature of Singaporean road signs is that they are always set on a square white background.
Rain trees are a common sight throughout Singapore, often planted along main roads.
It is common to see warnings written in large letters directly on the road, like the famous “HUMP AHEAD”.
Singaporean buses are easily recognizable, with most being lime-green. You might also see other designs, such as the white-and-purple SBS Transit buses.
All bus stops in Singapore are protected by concrete bollards with unique black-and-yellow warning bands.
Besides the bollards, some bus stops feature a unique yellow bus-leaving box with an arrow painted on the street.
Nearly all traffic lights in Singapore have a distinctive design, supported by a curved sheet of metal with several holes.
Many streets, particularly in the suburbs, are named after their neighbourhood (e.g., Street 31 in Ang Mo Kio). These neighbourhood names are useful for quickly locating yourself on the map.
The Tuas planning area is a recognizable industrial zone characterized by straight roads, industrial buildings, cranes, and shipping containers.
The island of Sentosa is recognizable by its green signposts, winding roads, and general resort atmosphere.
The Generation 3 trekker coverage on Pulau Ubin is identified by its unusually rural forest and a visible camouflage-style hat.
St. John and Lazarus Islands are recognizable by their Generation 3 trekker coverage, smooth asphalt roads, and the constant presence of the sea.
The tiny Kusu Island is easily identified by the red paving stones that make up all its pathways.
